content: Malaria remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in regions where it is endemic. Over the past decade, substantial progress in malaria control has been achieved, primarily through the use of long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs). However, the complete elimination of malaria has proven challenging, as current control measures fail to protect individuals from mosquito bites that occur outdoors or during periods of activity. Personal protection methods, such as repellents, may offer a solution during these vulnerable times. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of topical repellents, insecticide-treated clothing, and spatial repellents in reducing malaria transmission. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted up to June 26, 2017. These databases included the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, US AFPMB, CAB Abstracts, and LILACS. Additional searches were performed on trial registration platforms, conference proceedings, and through direct contact with organizations and companies to identify ongoing or unpublished trials. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) that assessed the use of topical repellents, permethrin-treated clothing, and spatial repellents such as mosquito coils. Trials were included regardless of whether they were conducted with or without LLINs. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer. Meta-analyses were conducted, and results were stratified based on the inclusion of LLINs. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of ten trials met the inclusion criteria, comprising eight cRCTs and two RCTs. These trials investigated three types of interventions: topical repellents (six trials), insecticide-treated clothing (two trials), and spatial repellents (two trials). Topical Repellents: Six trials, five of which were cluster-randomized, evaluated the use of topical repellents in malaria-endemic regions. Four of these trials combined topical repellents with LLINs, while two trials conducted in displaced populations used topical repellents alone. The evidence regarding the effectiveness of topical repellents in preventing clinical malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum was inconclusive (relative risk [RR] 0.65, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.40 to 1.07; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the evidence for preventing malaria infection caused by P. falciparum was uncertain (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.12; low-certainty evidence). For Plasmodium vivax, there was no clear evidence of protection against clinical cases (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.76; low-certainty evidence) or infection incidence (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.41; low-certainty evidence). Subgroup analyses of trials that included LLINs did not demonstrate a protective effect of topical repellents. Among the two trials that did not include LLINs, one reported a protective effect against clinical cases of P. falciparum (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.71), while the other found no protective effect against malaria infection caused by either P. falciparum or P. vivax. Insecticide-Treated Clothing: Two trials investigated the use of insecticide-treated clothing. These trials were conducted in refugee camps in Pakistan and among military personnel in the Colombian Amazon. Neither trial provided participants with LLINs. In the absence of LLINs, insecticide-treated clothing appeared to reduce the incidence of clinical malaria caused by P. falciparum by approximately 50% (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.83; low-certainty evidence). For P. vivax, the reduction in clinical malaria incidence was less pronounced and not statistically significant (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.01; low-certainty evidence). Spatial Repellents: Two cluster-randomized trials evaluated the use of mosquito coils as spatial repellents for malaria prevention. The effect of spatial repellents on malaria prevention remains uncertain (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.72; very low-certainty evidence). There was significant heterogeneity between the studies, and one study was assessed as having a high risk of bias. Conclusions: The evidence is insufficient to determine whether topical or spatial repellents are effective in preventing malaria. Better-designed trials are needed to provide higher-certainty evidence and to enable well-informed recommendations. Adherence to daily use of repellents remains a significant challenge. Insecticide-treated clothing may reduce the risk of malaria infection in the absence of LLINs, but further studies are required to evaluate its effectiveness in the general population and to expand the applicability of these findings.
